items.stem: A new engineer needs to understand why a firewall rule was configured unusually, and has time to research before touching anything. Which artifact should they consult?

options.text: Documentation — the descriptive record of what the system is and why, written for a reader who has time.
options.why: Documentation exists precisely to answer a why-question when there is time to read the answer.

options.text: The runbook covering this firewall, followed step by step, since it explains what to do rather than why the rule was configured this way.
options.why: A runbook instructs a reader under pressure; it deliberately does not explain why the system is built the way it is.

options.text: The change record showing when the rule was last edited and by whom, without stating why that decision was made or what depends on it.
options.why: Even a change record carrying a justification explains one past decision rather than the configuration standing today, and this one carries only who and when.

options.text: The monitoring dashboard for the firewall's current traffic, which shows values now rather than the reasoning behind the configuration.
options.why: A dashboard shows present values, not intent; it is not documentation even though it describes the system.

items.rationale: Documentation is descriptive reference material consulted by a reader who has time and context. A runbook is prescriptive and written for a stranger under pressure; a change record and a dashboard each capture a narrower fact and neither substitutes for a current-state description of the system and its rationale.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on first pass and fixed. Key holds: SP 800-128 treats the component inventory and baseline configuration as descriptive records of what a system is, distinct from the change-control record of what was altered; a runbook, a change record and a dashboard each answer a narrower question. The defect was o3's why, which asserted flatly that a change record never states why -- SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8 defines configuration change control as 'the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, test/evaluation, review, and disposition of changes', so justification is part of the record. The why was rewritten to rest on what the option text actually stipulates (who and when only) and on the true distinction that a justification explains one past decision rather than the configuration standing today. o2 and o4 are false as written and their whys are true. No distractor is also correct: each names an artifact that cannot answer a why-question in the scenario.

items.stem: A host has two hundred recorded changes in its history but no single document stating what the host currently runs or why. What is missing?

options.text: Documentation, since reconstructing current state from a change history is exactly the work it exists to save.
options.why: A stack of change records is not documentation, because nobody should have to replay history to learn what is true now.

options.text: Additional change records covering the gaps in the history, which still requires reconstructing the current state from that history.
options.why: More history still requires reconstruction; it does not itself state the current configuration and its rationale.

options.text: A runbook for restoring the host after a failure, which instructs what to do rather than describing what the host currently runs.
options.why: A runbook instructs what to do during an incident; it does not describe what the host is or why it is configured as it is.

options.text: Nothing — a complete change history is equivalent to documentation, since every past change is already recorded somewhere within it.
options.why: A change history and a current-state description answer different questions; one being complete does not produce the other.

items.rationale: Documentation states what is true now, kept next to the system it describes. A change history, however complete, records what happened over time and leaves reconstructing the present state as unfinished work — which is precisely the burden documentation removes.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.4 defines the component inventory as 'a descriptive record of the components within an organization', and sec. 2.3.7 defines a baseline configuration as a formally reviewed and agreed set of specifications 'used as a basis for future builds' -- both current-state artifacts, neither reconstructible for free from a change history. o2 (more change records), o3 (runbook) and o4 (history equals documentation) are each false, and each why states a true fact: more history still needs reconstruction; a runbook instructs rather than describes; completeness of a history does not produce a current-state description. No distractor is defensible as an answer.

items.stem: A team keeps every configuration change in Git and requires a reviewed pull request before merging. An auditor asks whether that is change management. What is missing?

options.text: Approval and scheduling for changes made by hand on a host, and an archived record for anything that never touches the repository.
options.why: Version control covers only what was committed; an unapproved change made directly on a host is still within change management's scope but outside the repository's.

options.text: Nothing — a reviewed pull request already satisfies change management, since every file change already passes through review.
options.why: Review gives history and attribution for files, but says nothing about impact review, scheduling, or approval of out-of-band changes.

options.text: The commit history itself, since it records what a file said and who wrote it, which is what version control already provides on its own.
options.why: That is what version control already provides; it is not the gap the auditor is asking about.

options.text: A defined maintenance window during which merges are permitted, which states only when work may happen rather than whether it was approved.
options.why: A window would state when work may happen, not whether it was reviewed and approved at all.

items.rationale: Change management is a human decision process producing an authorisation, distinct from the tool that stores the resulting file state. Git with reviewed pull requests gives history, attribution and file-level review; it does not by itself cover a hand-made change on a host or the impact review and archived approval a full process requires.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8 requires change control to cover 'emergency/unscheduled changes' and lists 'Requirements for retroactive analysis, testing, and approval of changes that are implemented' out of band, plus archiving of superseded baselines for audit traceability -- exactly the approval-plus-archived-record gap the key names, which a Git history cannot supply for a change never committed. o2 is false (review of files is not impact review or approval). o3's why is true: commit history is what version control already gives. o4 is not also correct -- a window permitting merges is a timing rule, and SP 800-128 places authorisation, not scheduling, at the centre of change control; the key already subsumes scheduling.

items.stem: An administrator proposes a configuration change and personally approves it before applying it to a system they run. Which control did the process fail to enforce?

options.text: Independent approval, meaning the approver must be someone other than the requestor.
options.why: Configuration change control requires a change to be vetted by an authorised individual independent of whoever proposed it.

options.text: Scheduling the change into an agreed maintenance window.
options.why: A window governs when disruptive work may occur; being inside one authorises nothing about whether the change was permitted at all.

options.text: Recording the change in a version-controlled repository.
options.why: Recording what changed is a separate concern from whether the change was authorised to happen.

options.text: Nothing — an administrator with authority over the system may approve their own change.
options.why: That is the exact self-approval the control forbids, regardless of how much authority the administrator holds.

items.rationale: The control that defines change management is independent approval: the requestor and the approver being different people. Scheduling and recording are separate concerns, and neither substitutes for a second, independent reviewer of the proposed change.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, and this is the strongest textual match in the file. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8: 'best practices for configuration change control require that changes to the system be vetted by at least one authorized individual who is independent of the requestor -- in other words, in order to maintain adequate separation of duties, system administrators, developers, etc., are not given the authority to unilaterally propose and approve changes'. That confirms the key verbatim in substance and confirms o4 as the exact prohibited case. o2 (window) and o3 (recording) are separate concerns and their whys are true; neither is also correct, since neither produces an authorisation.

items.stem: What is the "snowflake host" problem that standardization addresses?

options.text: A server built and maintained by hand, whose configuration exists nowhere but on the server itself, so no fix or script reliably applies to it.
options.why: That is the failure named by the practice: a one-off machine nobody dares touch because nothing about it is recorded elsewhere.

options.text: A host whose configuration-management tool has stopped converging it to the declared state, which is drift within an already-managed host.
options.why: That describes drift within a managed host, a narrower failure than a host that was never brought under management at all.

options.text: A host that falls short of the organisation's minimum secure configuration, which is a compliance gap rather than an unmanaged snowflake.
options.why: That is a security-baseline shortfall, a compliance question distinct from whether the host is configured like its peers at all.

options.text: Any host that has ever been patched by hand, even one whose configuration is otherwise fully recorded elsewhere and rebuildable from a known, reviewed specification.
options.why: One manual patch does not make a host unmanageable; the problem is a host whose configuration lives only on itself.

items.rationale: Standardization keeps machines of the same role configured alike so a fix, script or runbook applies to more than one host. The snowflake is the failure case: a hand-built server that works, that nobody dares touch, and whose configuration is recorded nowhere else.

verification.reasoning: Key holds on substance. SP 800-128 requires every configuration item to be the object of 'a documented and approved secure configuration' and defines the baseline as the basis for future builds; a host whose configuration exists only on itself is outside that regime, which is the failure the key describes. Caveat recorded honestly: the word 'snowflake' does not appear in SP 800-128 -- it is the guide's consensus vocabulary, and the citation supports the substance rather than the term. o2 (drift inside a managed host) and o3 (baseline shortfall) are narrower, distinct failures and their whys are true; SP 800-128 treats deviation-from-baseline as a separate, monitored condition. o4 is false: one manual patch does not remove a host from configuration control.

items.stem: A naming scheme fixes role, environment, region and an index in the same order for every host. Per consensus practice, what is that scheme's primary purpose?

options.text: To let a reader infer a host's identity and purpose from its name alone, without consulting anything else.
options.why: Names appear stripped of context in alerts and logs, so a reader typically has only the name to decide how to react.

options.text: To serve as the authoritative record of what a host is and who owns it, replacing the need to consult the inventory separately.
options.why: A name is a string someone typed and encodes information; it does not store it, so treating it as the authoritative record is the practice's usual failure mode.

options.text: To ensure no two hosts in the estate can ever hold the same name, which the register that assigns names enforces rather than the pattern those names follow.
options.why: Uniqueness across an estate is enforced by whatever assigns and records names; a convention only fixes the shape a name takes.

options.text: To guarantee that every host of a given role is configured identically, so a fix written for one of them applies unchanged to the rest.
options.why: That uniformity is standardization's goal; a naming scheme only makes identity readable, not configuration identical.

items.rationale: In most implementations of this consensus practice, a fixed, ordered naming scheme lets a reader decide from the name alone whether a host is production or test before deciding how urgently to react. The convention encodes information rather than storing it, so trusting a name as a record — of ownership or of anything else the inventory should carry — is exactly the failure mode the practice invites.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on first pass and fixed. Concept is waived in data/sourcing-waivers.json, so the claim rests on consensus practice and the LFCA competency list on the LF page (System Administration Fundamentals 30%, competency 'Best Practices'), which I fetched and read; it names the competency but no sub-topics. The defect was structural, not factual: o2 ('authoritative record ... replacing the inventory') and o3 ('the authoritative inventory of systems') asserted the same thing, letting a reader eliminate both on sight. o3 was rewritten to a distinct sibling claim about uniqueness enforcement, and o4 was lengthened with a real qualifying clause rather than the key being cut. Key, o2, o3 and o4 re-checked after the rewrite: exactly one is correct and all three whys state true facts.

items.stem: A script appends a configuration line to a file every time it runs, rather than checking whether the line is already present. It is scheduled nightly across fifty hosts. What results after a month?

options.text: Fifty files with duplicated entries; the script is fully automated but not idempotent.
options.why: Automation without idempotency multiplies a mistake instead of removing it, and appending unconditionally is exactly that mistake.

options.text: Convergence to a single declared state, because the script runs automatically every night.
options.why: Being automated says nothing about whether repeated runs are safe; convergence requires the operation itself to check state first.

options.text: No effect beyond the first run, because the change was already tested once before deployment.
options.why: A single successful test says nothing about what a second or hundredth run does; only re-running tests for idempotency.

options.text: Nothing unusual — since the script is automated, running it repeatedly is inherently safe.
options.why: Idempotency is a property of how the operation is written, not a consequence of it being scheduled or automated.

items.rationale: Automation replaces a manual procedure with a script; idempotency is the separate property that running it twice leaves the same end state with no further change. An unconditional append is automated and not idempotent, and re-running it across a fleet turns one mistake into fifty.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. The Ansible glossary defines idempotency as: 'An operation is idempotent if the result of performing it once is exactly the same as the result of performing it repeatedly without any intervening actions.' An unconditional append fails that test, so fifty nightly runs accumulate duplicates -- automated, not idempotent. o2 is false: the glossary attributes convergence to resource models that 'are idempotent meaning change commands are not run unless needed', a property of how the operation is written, not of scheduling. o3 and o4 are false and their whys are true. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A configuration script is re-run against a host and reports that zero changes were made. What does that result indicate?

options.text: The system already matched the intended state; a no-op second run is the signal of success, not evidence the tool did nothing useful.
options.why: An idempotent operation is expected to report no change once the desired state is already in force.

options.text: The configuration-management tool has failed to detect drift, since a healthy tool is expected to report and correct differences every run.
options.why: Detecting no drift and reporting no change is the tool working correctly, not a detection failure.

options.text: An alerting threshold has not yet been crossed, which belongs to a separate practice concerned with notifying someone of a breached condition.
options.why: Thresholds and alert conditions belong to a different practice entirely and are not what a script's change count reports.

options.text: The script has not yet been validated in a staging environment, which is a question about where it was tested rather than what it changed.
options.why: Where a script was validated is unrelated to what a specific run against a specific host reports.

items.rationale: Idempotent work is typically written as a check followed by a conditional action, or expressed declaratively. A second run reporting no changes is exactly the signal that the system already matches intent, and is read as success rather than as the tool having done nothing useful.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. The Ansible glossary's resource-model entry states that change commands 'are not run unless needed' and that Ansible brings the system to the desired state regardless of actual state; a zero-change second run is therefore the expected report once intent is already in force, not a null result. o2 inverts that and is false, o3 (alert thresholds) and o4 (staging validation) are unrelated to what a run reports, and all three whys state true facts. No distractor is defensible.

items.stem: Which question does configuration management answer, as distinct from infrastructure as code?

options.text: Is this machine configured as declared, rather than whether the machine exists at all.
options.why: Configuration management acts on the state inside systems that already exist; it configures rather than creates.

options.text: Does this environment exist as declared.
options.why: That is infrastructure as code's question: whether the infrastructure itself has been brought into existence.

options.text: Is this operation safe to run a second time.
options.why: That is a property of a single procedure, which is what automation and idempotency addresses, not the scope of configuration management.

options.text: Both ask the same question, since both keep declarations in version control and both re-apply to converge.
options.why: The shared vocabulary is exactly why they are confusable, but one configures what exists and the other creates what does not yet exist.

items.rationale: Configuration management declares and enforces the state inside systems that already exist. Infrastructure as code decides whether the infrastructure itself exists. Both are declarative and both re-apply to converge, which is exactly what makes the pair easy to conflate.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 scopes security-focused configuration management to establishing, enforcing and monitoring approved configurations of systems and their configuration items -- state inside systems that already exist -- and never to provisioning the infrastructure itself. o2 states infrastructure as code's question and its why is true. o3's why correctly assigns re-runnability to idempotency, a property of one procedure. o4 is false: shared declarative vocabulary does not make the two questions the same. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: After a configuration-management playbook is run against a hand-edited host, an operator claims the host now matches the approved baseline. What limits that claim?

options.text: Only the settings the declaration mentions are corrected; anything it never mentions survives untouched.
options.why: "We ran the playbook" is not the same claim as "the host now matches the baseline" for exactly this reason.

options.text: Baselines are enforced only through configuration management and never through a published, independently maintained industry benchmark.
options.why: Baselines are commonly derived from published benchmarks first and only then held in place by a tool; this reverses that relationship.

options.text: The claim can only be verified once a monitoring alert fires.
options.why: Compliance with a declared baseline is checked by re-applying the declaration, not by waiting for an alert condition.

options.text: Nothing limits it — a playbook run always brings every setting into full compliance.
options.why: A declaration only corrects what it mentions; settings outside its scope are left exactly as the hand edit left them.

items.rationale: The tool changes only what the declaration mentions. Anything a hand edit touched outside that scope survives the run untouched, which is why running the playbook and matching the baseline are different claims.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. A declaration corrects only the settings it names; SP 800-128 accordingly treats deviation detection as a separate monitoring activity ('documentation of deviations from the baseline configuration', integrity checks against the baseline) rather than something a single apply-run guarantees. o2's why is confirmed by SP 800-128 sec. 3.1.1: a common secure configuration is 'a recognized, standardized, and established benchmark (e.g., National Checklist Program, DISA STIGs)' used as the basis for approved baselines, so baselines derive from published benchmarks and are then held by a tool -- the option reverses this and is false. o3 and o4 are false with true whys.

items.stem: A team reverts a bad commit in their configuration repository. What is true immediately afterward?

options.text: The declaration has changed back; nothing on any host changes until the reverted state is re-applied.
options.why: Reverting a commit changes the declaration, not the running system.

options.text: The running system is restored to the previous state, as if reverting a commit undid the change on every host that was running it.
options.why: "We reverted it" describes an intention restored, not an outage ended; the host is untouched until something re-applies the declaration.

options.text: A restorable snapshot of the affected host has been created automatically, independent of anything recorded in the repository itself.
options.why: A revert changes a file in a repository; it does not capture a copy of any running system.

options.text: The change has been approved for release, as though editing the repository were itself the independent review step it requires.
options.why: Reverting a commit is an edit to the declaration, not an approval decision made by an independent reviewer.

items.rationale: Version control preserves changes as someone meant them, and a revert is one more such change. The limit is precise: reverting alters the declaration, and nothing happens on any host until a tool or a person re-applies it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. The declaration-versus-running-system split is the same one SP 800-128 draws when it says superseded baselines are retained so that 'retention of previous versions allows for a rollback or restoration to a previous secure and functional version' -- the stored version enables a restoration, it does not perform one. Caveat recorded: the phrase 'version control' does not occur in SP 800-128; the citation supports the substance through baseline versioning and rollback, not the tooling term. o2 is false, and o3 and o4 are false with true whys (a revert captures no running state and is not an approval decision). No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A change has passed every test in staging but has no documented way to be undone. What is still true about its risk?

options.text: The risk remains unbounded; testing reduces the chance of a break, but only a rollback path bounds the damage if it happens anyway.
options.why: The two halves are separately examinable: testing lowers the odds of failure, and a rollback path limits the consequence of one.

options.text: The risk is fully mitigated, since a pre-change snapshot always accompanies staging tests.
options.why: Testing establishes nothing about whether a restorable copy exists; the two are separate disciplines.

options.text: The risk is eliminated, because staging testing already proved the change safe under every condition production could present.
options.why: A test reduces the chance of failure; it does not bound the damage of the failure it missed.

options.text: The risk is bounded by the maintenance window the change will run inside, which limits only when the work happens, not how far it spreads.
options.why: A window governs when disruptive work may happen, not how far the damage from a failed change can spread.

items.rationale: Testing and a rollback path address different failure moments: testing tries to prevent the break, and the rollback path bounds it if testing missed something. A tested change with no way back is still an unbounded risk.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8 lists as separate change-control requirements both testing/evaluation before release into the operational environment and 'Requirements for rollback of changes in the event that problems occur' -- two distinct obligations, which is exactly the key's claim that testing lowers the odds while only a rollback path bounds the damage. o2 is false (testing establishes nothing about a restorable copy), o3 is false (no test proves safety under every production condition), o4 is false (a window governs timing, not blast radius). All three whys are true.

items.stem: A dashboard displays CPU, memory and error rate for every host, but nobody is subscribed to any notification channel. A service is down for six hours before anyone notices. Which discipline is missing?

options.text: Alerting — collection ran and the evidence exists, but nobody was interrupted in time to act on it.
options.why: Monitoring observes; alerting interrupts. A dashboard nobody watches detects nothing at the moment it matters.

options.text: Logging — the systemd journal was not queried during the outage.
options.why: A local log store is read after someone already suspects a problem; it is not the mechanism that raises the suspicion in the first place.

options.text: Capacity planning — the growth trend toward exhaustion was never projected.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario describes a resource trending toward a ceiling; the failure is that nobody was told about an active outage.

options.text: Nothing is missing — a dashboard collecting metrics is monitoring and alerting together.
options.why: Collection without a notification path that reaches someone obliged to answer is monitoring alone, and detects nothing unattended.

items.rationale: Monitoring is continuous collection; alerting is the notification that interrupts a human when a condition is breached. A dashboard nobody watches makes evidence available afterward but detects nothing at the moment it happens, which is the gap alerting exists to close.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, and the citation was strengthened. SP 800-128 sec. 3.4 describes automated tools that 'monitor systems for changes and alert system staff', separating collection from notification. Google SRE ch. 11 supplies the human-interruption half directly ('Paging alerts should be aligned with the symptoms that threaten a service's SLOs'), and google-sre-book-being-on-call was added to source_ids because SP 800-128 alone does not carry it. o2 (journald), o3 (capacity planning) and o4 (dashboard equals alerting) are false, and each why states a true fact. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A low-severity alert fires every few minutes for a condition that needs no action, until the on-call channel mutes all notifications from it. A real outage is later missed. What failed?

options.text: Alert quality — a condition that needed no action trained people to ignore the channel, so the next real alert was dismissed too.
options.why: Alerting on conditions that need no action is the reverse failure to under-alerting, and it is just as examinable.

options.text: The runbook for the outage was never written, leaving nobody with a step-by-step procedure to follow once the outage was noticed.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario turns on whether a procedure existed; the failure is that the alert was never seen at all.

options.text: The outage happened outside an agreed maintenance window, so the disruption itself was never pre-agreed with the people it affected.
options.why: Whether disruptive work is scheduled is unrelated to why an unscheduled outage's alert was ignored.

options.text: Escalation — the notification reached an unstaffed channel, so nobody was ever in a position to see it fire in the first place.
options.why: That is a different, real failure mode this practice also names, but it is not what is described: the channel was staffed, and was muted deliberately.

items.rationale: Alerting on conditions that need no action trains people to ignore alerts, so the next genuine one is dismissed with it. The distinguishing feature here is that the channel was staffed and reachable — the failure is alert quality, not the separate case of a notification reaching nobody.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on first pass for attribution and fixed; prose unchanged because the claim is true. The item turned on alert fatigue, and NIST SP 800-128 -- which it cited -- contains no such material (no occurrence of alert fatigue, false-positive alerting, or non-actionable alerts; its only 'false positive' passage concerns configuration-scanning tools). Google SRE ch. 11 states it exactly: 'All paging alerts should also be actionable. Low-priority alerts that bother the on-call engineer every hour ... the fatigue such alerts induce can also cause serious alerts to be treated with less attention than necessary.' source_ids corrected to lf-objectives-2025 plus google-sre-book-being-on-call. Key re-verified against that text; o2, o3 and o4 are false with true whys, and o4 is correctly distinguished because the scenario's channel was staffed and deliberately muted.

items.stem: An alert fires when a disk reaches 85% usage. Is that capacity planning?

options.text: No — that is monitoring and alerting reporting the present; capacity planning projects the trend forward to the date the disk will be full.
options.why: An 85% alert is a statement about now; deciding when the array will be full and arranging expansion is a statement about the future made from the same data.

options.text: Yes — any statement referencing a resource threshold counts as capacity planning, regardless of whether it describes now or a future planning date.
options.why: A threshold crossed now is exactly the present-tense statement capacity planning is distinguished from.

options.text: No — it is asset and inventory management confirming the volume exists, which records what systems exist rather than how full they are.
options.why: The alert says nothing about whether the volume is recorded in an inventory; it reports a usage level.

options.text: Yes — the 85% figure defines the maintenance window for the expansion work, rather than describing the disk's condition today.
options.why: A threshold alert states a current condition; it does not by itself schedule a window for future work.

items.rationale: Per consensus practice, monitoring reports a value now and alerts when a threshold is crossed — a statement about the present. Capacity planning extrapolates historical utilisation forward against a known ceiling to produce a date, which is what makes procurement and a maintenance window schedulable before they become urgent. The two are complementary, and the planning is only as good as the history the monitoring retained.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. Concept is waived, so the claim rests on consensus practice; the LF page was read and confirms only that 'Best Practices' is a competency of System Administration Fundamentals (30%). The present-versus-future distinction is sound and matches the guide: a threshold alert reports a value now, capacity planning extrapolates retained history against a ceiling to produce a date. o2 is false (a crossed threshold is the present-tense statement being distinguished), o3 and o4 are false, and all three whys state true facts. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A change is applied inside an agreed maintenance window but was never reviewed or approved beforehand. Is the change authorised?

options.text: No. A window states only when disruptive work may occur, not whether it may happen at all.
options.why: Approval and scheduling are two different boundaries, and being inside the window authorises nothing on its own.

options.text: Yes — being inside the agreed window is itself the authorisation.
options.why: An unapproved change does not become permissible because it was applied inside an agreed period for disruptive work.

options.text: Only if the change's requestor is also its approver.
options.why: That describes the exact self-approval an independent-review control forbids; it does not grant authorisation.

options.text: Yes, provided the change is routine rather than an emergency fix.
options.why: Whether a change follows a routine or an expedited schedule is a cadence question, not a substitute for review and approval.

items.rationale: A maintenance window is an agreed period for disruptive work, communicated in advance to those it affects. It answers when work may be done, not whether it was ever approved — an unapproved change does not become permissible because the calendar allowed it.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on first pass for attribution and fixed; prose unchanged. SP 800-40r4 supports the window half only loosely -- it speaks of a 'scheduled outage window' and 'scheduled downtime for maintenance' and never uses the term maintenance window -- and contains nothing about whether a change was authorised, which is what the key turns on. nist-sp-800-128 was added to source_ids because it carries that claim: change control requires vetting by an authorised individual independent of the requestor, and separately requires management of unscheduled changes with expedited reviews and approvals. Key re-verified. o2 is the exact conflation the source forbids; o3's why is true (self-approval is prohibited, and it grants nothing here); o4's why is true and matches SP 800-40r4's routine-versus-emergency scenarios, which are cadence distinctions rather than authorisation.

items.stem: An administrator holds root on every host in the fleet, but the change process still requires someone else to approve any change that administrator proposes. What does that arrangement demonstrate?

options.text: Separation of duties — no single identity, however privileged, can both make and approve a change alone.
options.why: It is a structural control on how many identities a workflow requires, independent of how much any one of them is trusted.

options.text: Least privilege — the administrator's access has been scoped to what the role needs.
options.why: Least privilege is about the size of one identity's authority; root on every host is the opposite of a scoped grant.

options.text: Role-based deprovisioning, since the administrator's excess privilege will eventually be revoked once their role changes again.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario describes revoking access on a role change; the control shown operates at the moment of the change itself.

options.text: Nothing structural — the control applies only to staff below root, so an administrator holding root on every host falls outside its reach entirely.
options.why: The control constrains how many identities a workflow requires, and it is not waived by how privileged any one of those identities happens to be.

items.rationale: Separation of duties splits a sensitive workflow so no single person can complete it alone, regardless of that person's privilege. Least privilege is a different axis entirely — the size of one identity's authority — and an administrator with root on every host still cannot self-approve a change where duties are genuinely separated.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on first pass and fixed. Key holds: SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8 names the arrangement outright -- vetting by an authorized individual independent of the requestor is required 'in order to maintain adequate separation of duties' -- and SP 800-53r5 AC-5 describes separation of duties as dividing functions among different individuals to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion, a structural control independent of privilege level. The defect was that o2 and o4 both headlined 'Least privilege', letting a reader eliminate both on sight because only one option can be right. o4 was rewritten to a distinct misconception (that the control does not reach a root-holding administrator), which AC-5 and SP 800-128 both falsify. Key, o2, o3 and o4 re-checked after the rewrite: exactly one is correct and all three whys state true facts.

items.stem: A responder unfamiliar with a system is paged at 03:00 to restore a service that has failed. Which artifact should they follow?

options.text: The runbook, a numbered, sequential procedure with an expected result at each step, written for exactly this situation.
options.why: A runbook is instruction rather than explanation, written to be followed under pressure by someone who may not know the system.

options.text: Documentation — it explains why the system is built the way it is.
options.why: Documentation is descriptive and assumes a reader with time; handed to someone at 03:00 who has never seen the system, an explanation is close to useless.

options.text: The disaster recovery plan governing activation criteria and notification.
options.why: That plan is broader and governs whether a disaster is declared and who is told; the runbook is the procedure layer inside it, and is what this task needs.

options.text: Any document describing the system, since documentation and runbooks serve the same purpose under pressure.
options.why: They are read by the same kind of person at the worst possible time, but one instructs and the other explains, and only one is safe to follow blind.

items.rationale: The conditions a runbook is used under are the conditions people reason worst in. It is written as a sequential procedure with no step assumed, precisely because a step obvious to the author is the step a stranger will get wrong at night.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, with a near-verbatim match. SP 800-34r1 sec. 4: 'Plans should be formatted to provide quick and clear directions in the event that personnel unfamiliar with the plan or the systems are called on to perform recovery operations ... Where possible, checklists and step-by-step procedures should be used', and recovery procedures are 'written at a level that an appropriately skilled technician can recover the system without intimate system knowledge'. o2 (documentation) is false for a 03:00 stranger and its why is true. o3's why is true: the contingency plan governs activation and notification, with procedures as the layer inside it. o4 is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A runbook has sat in the team wiki for two years and has never once been executed. What is the state of its reliability?

options.text: Unknown. An untested runbook is an assumption, since its steps rot silently as the system changes.
options.why: The correct maintenance of a runbook is exercising it, not merely storing it, and the moment of real use is the worst time to discover it has rotted.

options.text: Verified, since testing before production would have caught any drift.
options.why: That practice tests whether a change is safe to deploy; it does not exercise whether a stored procedure's steps still match the system.

options.text: Verified, since the documentation for the same system is kept current.
options.why: Documentation staying current says nothing about whether a separate, unexecuted procedure still works.

options.text: Reliable — storing the procedure correctly is what maintaining a runbook means.
options.why: Storage is not maintenance; a runbook's steps can silently stop matching the system it describes.

items.rationale: A runbook that has never been exercised is an assumption about whether its steps still work, not evidence that they do. Systems change underneath stored procedures, and the moment someone needs the runbook is the worst possible time to discover a step no longer applies.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-34r1 sec. 3.6 requires the plan to be 'maintained in a ready state that accurately reflects system requirements, procedures, organizational structure, and policies' precisely because systems 'undergo frequent changes', and its FAQ states the plan should be reviewed at least annually and on significant change, with 'deficiencies identified through testing' addressed in maintenance -- i.e. testing, not storage, is what establishes that steps still work. An unexercised two-year-old runbook therefore has unknown reliability. o2, o3 and o4 are false and their whys are true.

items.stem: A host is compromised, and nobody remembers it exists — it was never entered into any system record. What discipline's absence does that reveal?

options.text: Asset and inventory management — you cannot patch, secure or decommission what you do not know about.
options.why: The dangerous host is always the one nobody remembered, which is exactly what a maintained inventory exists to prevent.

options.text: Monitoring and alerting — the host should have triggered a threshold alert.
options.why: Monitoring watches only the systems someone configured it to watch, which by construction excludes a forgotten host.

options.text: Security baselines — the host fell below the minimum secure configuration.
options.why: A baseline shortfall assumes the host is already known and enrolled; the failure here happened before that point.

options.text: Nothing is missing — the compromise itself is an adequate discovery mechanism.
options.why: Discovering a host only once it is attacked is the failure state the practice exists to avoid, not a substitute for it.

items.rationale: The inventory is the prerequisite every other discipline in this competency quietly assumes: patch cadence applies to the estate it lists, baselines are enforced on the hosts it names, and monitoring watches what it was told exists. A host outside that record is invisible to all of them.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.4: the component inventory 'is a descriptive record of the components within an organization down to the system level', and a consolidated view 'allows the organization to have greater visibility into and control over its systems, facilitating the implementation, operation, and management of a security program' -- a host absent from it is outside all of that. o2's why is true (monitoring watches only what it was configured to watch), o3's why is true (a baseline shortfall presumes enrolment), o4 is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: Two servers of the same role differ because two different engineers each made their own configuration choices, and neither choice was ever reviewed. What discipline's absence explains this?

options.text: Security baselines — a reviewed, approved minimum configuration removes security from the discretion of whoever happened to build the machine.
options.why: Without a baseline, the question "is this host secure" is answerable only by opinion; a baseline makes it answerable by comparison.

options.text: Standardization — the servers should be rebuilt from a single golden image, which gives uniformity but not a reviewed security floor.
options.why: Standardization is the general uniformity goal; the specific control missing here is a reviewed, approved security floor.

options.text: Configuration management — a tool should have converged both servers automatically, once someone declared a state for it to enforce.
options.why: A tool enforces whatever state is declared; it does not by itself supply the reviewed security minimum that state should contain.

options.text: Nothing is missing — a system running more security controls than another is still compliant.
options.why: Compliance is measured against the defined floor, not against how a system compares to a less-secure neighbour.

items.rationale: A security baseline is a defined minimum configuration, formally reviewed and agreed, applied to every system of a given type. It removes security decisions from individual discretion, which is exactly what two divergent, unreviewed configurations of the same role indicates is missing.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.7 defines a baseline configuration as 'a set of specifications for a system, or Configuration Item within a system, that has been formally reviewed and agreed on at a given point in time, and which can be changed only through change control procedures' -- the reviewed, approved floor the key names, which is exactly what two engineers' unreviewed divergent choices lack. o2's why is true (standardization is the uniformity goal, not a reviewed security floor). o3's why is true: SP 800-128 has the tool enforce a declared state and takes the secure minimum from common secure configurations and benchmarks. o4 is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A departing employee's Unix login account is disabled the same day they leave. Is offboarding complete?

options.text: No. SSH keys, API tokens, VPN certificates, third-party accounts and shared secrets typically survive the disabling of that one account.
options.why: Disabling the login account is not revoking access; everything held outside that account survives its disabling untouched.

options.text: Yes — disabling the primary login account revokes everything that identity could do, since no other credential is able to outlive that one account.
options.why: An enumerated list of everything an identity can hold typically extends well beyond the one account that was disabled.

options.text: Yes — least privilege already limited what that account could reach, so nothing further needs to be revoked once the person departs.
options.why: Least privilege bounds how much an identity holds at any moment; offboarding is the separate question of completely removing what it holds when it departs.

options.text: No — the account must first be added to the asset inventory, before any credential attached to the departing employee can be revoked.
options.why: The inventory records systems and ownership; it is not a prerequisite for revoking a departing employee's credentials.

items.rationale: Onboarding failures announce themselves within the hour; offboarding failures are silent, because a credential still valid and attached to nobody is watched by nobody. Disabling the login account is only the start — installed keys, tokens, certificates and shared secrets all typically outlive it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, confirmed against the control text. SP 800-53r5 PS-4 lists as separate required actions on termination: '(a) Disable system access within [time period]' and '(b) Terminate or revoke any authenticators and credentials associated with the individual', with the discussion enumerating hardware authentication tokens, keys, cards and passes as retrievable property. Disabling one login account is therefore explicitly not the whole obligation, which falsifies o2. o3's why is true (least privilege bounds what an identity holds; offboarding removes it). o4 is false: no inventory entry is a precondition for revocation under PS-4. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A pre-change snapshot is taken immediately before a risky migration. A week later, the migration is confirmed good. What typically happens to that copy?

options.text: It is often discarded, since it existed to undo one identified action rather than to satisfy ongoing retention.
options.why: That is what distinguishes it from the scheduled backup regime, which protects against loss over time rather than one change.

options.text: It automatically becomes part of the routine, retention-scheduled backup regime.
options.why: A pre-change copy exists to undo one identified action; routine backups are a separate, ongoing regime sized by a recovery point objective.

options.text: It must be kept indefinitely, since any pre-change copy is a permanent compliance record.
options.why: The change record states where the copy is and how long it is kept, and that period is typically short, not indefinite.

options.text: It is deleted immediately once the change is applied, before the outcome is confirmed.
options.why: Deleting it before the change is confirmed good would remove the only rollback that does not depend on the change going as planned.

items.rationale: A pre-change copy is tied to one specific change and is often discarded once that change is confirmed good, unlike a routine backup sized against an ongoing recovery point objective. The copy is only useful while the change it guards against remains unconfirmed.

verification.reasoning: Key holds as hedged. SP 800-128 sec. 2.3.8 requires 'rollback of changes in the event that problems occur', which is the single-change purpose the key rests on, and SP 800-34r1 (with SP 800-53r5 CP-9) sizes the routine regime by organisation-defined backup frequency and recovery point objective -- confirming o2's why that the two regimes are different things. The disposition claim is deliberately hedged ('often discarded') and no source contradicts it for a per-change copy; recorded honestly, no cited source states a retention rule for pre-change copies, and SP 800-128's nearest analogue concerns archiving superseded baselines, not host snapshots. o3 and o4 are false and their whys are true. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: An organisation patches monthly and has no way for an actively exploited vulnerability to bypass that schedule. What is missing from their patch cadence?

options.text: An expedited path — a cadence with no emergency route leaves an actively exploited vulnerability waiting for the calendar.
options.why: "We patch monthly" does not describe a complete cadence without a named exception for a fix that cannot wait.

options.text: An inventory of patchable assets, since cadence is one decision inside the whole tracking-testing-applying-verifying practice.
options.why: That names the broader patch management practice cadence sits inside; the specific gap described is the missing exception path, not asset tracking.

options.text: A defined maintenance window for the monthly cycle.
options.why: A monthly window already exists in the scenario; the gap is the exception path for something that cannot wait for it.

options.text: Nothing — a monthly schedule with no exception path is still a complete cadence.
options.why: A critical security fix is expected to leave the routine schedule rather than wait for it, which a schedule with no exception cannot do.

items.rationale: Patch cadence is the rhythm updates are applied on, together with the expedited path critical fixes take when they cannot wait for it. A schedule that never states that exception leaves an actively exploited vulnerability exposed for the length of a full cycle.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. SP 800-40r4 sec. 3.4-3.5 requires organisations to define separate risk-response scenarios, with routine patching for 'patches that are on a regular release cycle and have not been elevated to emergency status' and a distinct emergency patching scenario run on 'a highly accelerated schedule'; it also notes automation 'is also needed for emergency situations, like patching a severe vulnerability that attackers are actively exploiting'. A cadence with no such exception is therefore incomplete, and o4 is false. o2's why is true (asset inventory is the surrounding practice, not the described gap) and o3's why is true (a monthly window already exists in the scenario). No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A patch is deployed first to a small set of canary systems, then to the rest of the estate once no breakage appears. Which decision does that phasing belong to?

options.text: Patch cadence — the scheduling decision for how and when updates roll out, including the order deployment follows.
options.why: Even routine deployment is normally phased, and the order it follows is part of the cadence decision, not a separate practice.

options.text: Patch management as a whole, since testing, deployment and verification are all part of the wider practice.
options.why: Naming the whole surrounding practice loses the specific decision the question asks about — the rollout order is one decision inside it.

options.text: Testing before production, since canaries function as a staging environment.
options.why: Canary systems are live production hosts receiving the real patch, not an isolated environment used before production is touched.

options.text: Maintenance windows, since canaries define which hosts fall inside the agreed window.
options.why: A window governs when disruptive work may occur; it does not decide which hosts receive a phased rollout first.

items.rationale: Patch cadence names the scheduling decision inside patch management: how often updates go out and, within that, the order a rollout follows. Canary-first deployment is a cadence-level rollout decision, distinct from the broader practice, from pre-production testing in an isolated environment, and from the timing question a maintenance window answers.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, and I checked the one place it could have failed. SP 800-40r4 sec. 3.5.1 places canary rounds inside the maintenance plan for a rollout: canaries identify likely operational impact, 'the deployment can expand to more or all of the vulnerable assets', and larger rollouts use 'multiple rounds of canary assets' -- a scheduling and ordering decision. The source also says of canaries 'In effect, this is how the patching gets tested', which is why o3 needed care: o3 is nevertheless false as written because it claims canaries function as a staging environment, whereas SP 800-40r4's canaries are live assets belonging to real users (administrators first, then early adopters across the organisation). o3's why states that correctly. o2 names the whole surrounding practice rather than the decision asked about; o4 is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: Per consensus practice, what trade-off does the principle of least astonishment argue for?

options.text: Conventional, expected defaults over clever or unusual configurations, because a surprising setup fails badly when nobody has time to read during an incident.
options.why: It argues for behaving the way an experienced administrator would expect, precisely because incidents leave no time to discover a surprise.

options.text: Optimised, non-standard configurations, since performance should take priority over convention even when the result surprises an operator.
options.why: That is the opposite trade-off from the one this principle argues for; it favours the conventional choice over the clever one.

options.text: Identical configuration across every host regardless of role, so that no two machines of any kind are ever allowed to differ.
options.why: Uniformity across hosts of the same role is standardization's claim, not what this principle argues for.

options.text: An enforceable minimum configuration, reviewed and approved centrally, rather than a design preference recognised by convention alone.
options.why: That describes a baseline; this principle is a design preference for unsurprising behaviour, not an enforceable control.

items.rationale: Per consensus practice, the principle of least astonishment argues for conventional defaults over clever ones, because a surprising setup fails during incidents when nobody has time to read. It is a design preference recognised at recall level, not an enforceable control like a baseline.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. Concept is waived in data/sourcing-waivers.json (no citable primary source; authoritative references paywalled), so this is a consensus-practice recall item, and the LF page was fetched and confirms only the competency's existence and weight. The trade-off named is the standard one and is stated consistently in the guide. o2 is the exact inversion; o3 belongs to standardization; o4 describes an enforceable baseline rather than a design preference. All three whys state true facts, and no distractor is defensible as the trade-off this principle argues for.

items.stem: Per consensus practice, what does having a named owner for a service establish, as distinct from the on-call responder or the asset record?

options.text: Accountability for the service's health, cost and lifecycle over its life, not just handling one incident or recording its existence.
options.why: The owner is accountable across the service's whole life, which is a different role from the responder handling a single incident.

options.text: The same accountability as the on-call responder, since both may be contacted during an incident.
options.why: Being reachable during an incident is not the same as holding ongoing accountability for the service's health, cost and lifecycle.

options.text: A record of the service's existence, indistinguishable from its inventory entry, rather than an accountability held by any one person.
options.why: The inventory stores the service's name and details; ownership is the accountability attached to it, not the record itself.

options.text: Responsibility for revoking the service's credentials when staff depart, which belongs to the separate offboarding process instead.
options.why: Revoking credentials on departure is offboarding's job; service ownership is accountable for the service, not for that specific process.

items.rationale: Per consensus practice, every service has a named owner accountable for its health, cost and lifecycle, so nothing is silently unmaintained. That is distinct from the on-call responder, who handles one incident, and from the asset record, which stores the name rather than the accountability.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. Concept is waived, so the claim rests on consensus practice; the LF page was fetched and confirms the competency only. Ownership as lifetime accountability is distinct from the on-call responder's per-incident role -- a distinction Google SRE ch. 11 also draws when it scopes on-call to handling incidents within a shift -- and distinct from the inventory record. o2, o3 and o4 are false and their whys state true facts. No distractor is also correct.
